headline_seed: Tropical Storm Moke to cause more flooding as Hawaii recovers from Lala - NPR

consensus_facts: Tropical Storm Moke is approaching Hawaii and is forecast to pass to the south of the Hawaiian islands rather than make landfall (NPR, Al Jazeera, CNN, Newsweek).

Moke arrives less than a week after Hurricane/Tropical Storm Lala struck Hawaii, and its rainfall threat is amplified because it falls on already-saturated, recently-flooded ground (NPR, Al Jazeera, CNN, Newsweek).

The National Hurricane Center warned the rainfall may produce 'life-threatening flooding and mudslides' for the windward and southeast Big Island, especially in steep/deep terrain and areas recently affected by Lala (NPR, CNN, Newsweek).
Up to 15 inches of rain is possible on the Big Island, with eastern Maui expecting roughly 3 to 6 inches (NPR, CNN, Newsweek).

Lala did not make landfall but dropped extreme rainfall — reported at more than 30 inches / roughly 39 inches / over 3.5 feet in some areas — triggering floods and mudslides that damaged roads, bridges and homes (NPR, Al Jazeera, Newsweek).
At least one person died in connection with Lala (NPR, Al Jazeera, Newsweek).

Lala caused widespread power outages, with reports of roughly 100,000 to 130,000 utility customers losing power (Al Jazeera, Newsweek; NPR reports more than 8,000 still without power as of Saturday morning).
Local officials urged residents to prepare for Moke and warned of hazardous conditions, power and communication interruptions (NPR, Newsweek).
The NHC advisory referenced was issued at 11 p.m. local time Saturday (NPR, Newsweek).

disagreements.topic: Lower-bound / total rainfall amounts for Moke on the Big Island

positions.NPR: States up to 15 inches could fall across the Big Island (no explicit lower range).
positions.CNN: Five to 10 inches expected on the Big Island, with up to 15 inches possible on central and eastern slopes.
positions.Newsweek: 5 to 10 inches spanning, with up to 15 inches in some locations.
3 to 6 inches on average for eastern Maui.

disagreements.topic: Cause of the single Lala fatality

positions.NPR: A 90-year-old woman died in a flood caused by the hurricane, per Hawaii Public Radio.
positions.Newsweek: Governor Josh Green said one person died in a weather-related car crash.
positions.Al Jazeera: At least one person died in last weekend's storm (no cause specified).

disagreements.topic: Number without power / outage figures from Lala

positions.NPR: More than 8,000 still without power as of Saturday morning; full restoration not expected until Sept. 8.

disagreements.topic: Moke's maximum sustained winds on Saturday

positions.Newsweek: Winds of 45 mph on Saturday evening.

disagreements.topic: Distance of Moke's closest approach to the Big Island

positions.Al Jazeera: About 684 km (425 miles) south of Hilo as of 11 a.m. HST Saturday.
positions.CNN: Center about 250 miles south of the Big Island later Sunday during closest approach.

disagreements.topic: Classification of Lala at the time it struck

positions.NPR: A hurricane, now downgraded to a tropical storm.
positions.Newsweek: Downgraded to a tropical storm by the time it struck; refers to it as Tropical Storm Lala.

framing_analysis.Associated Press (wire): Body text is essentially only photo captions (NOAA satellite image, debris in Naalehu, washed-out roads, damaged auto shop). No substantive reporting retrievable — frames the story visually around Lala's aftermath damage rather than Moke's forecast. Effectively headline-plus-captions only.
framing_analysis.NPR (lean-left): Leads on the recovery-during-a-new-threat angle. Emphasizes human and infrastructure impact: 8,000 without power, Sept. 8 restoration date, the 90-year-old flood victim, the governor's emergency request, and the county mayor's warning. Includes cross-links to its own prior Lala coverage. Straightforward wire-style tone with a public-safety focus.
framing_analysis.Al Jazeera English (international): Leads with precise storm metrics — coordinates, distance from Hilo, speed, wind speed in metric-first units — reflecting an international audience. Frames Lala's damage in scale (39 inches rain, 130,000 without power) but omits official statements from Hawaiian leaders and the specific fatality detail.
framing_analysis.CNN (lean-left): Files under a 'climate' URL and leads on the meteorological mechanism — why saturated ground and steep terrain make less rain more dangerous. Most technical forecast detail (flood watch, wind advisory zones, gust speeds, closest-approach distances, Volcanoes National Park closure). Emphasizes the compounding-threat science over politics or casualties.
framing_analysis.Newsweek: Leads on the 'life-threatening' warning framing and a tracker-map hook. Broadest context: situates Moke and Lala within the 2026 Pacific/Atlantic season, invokes El Niño and warmer ocean waters, notes no Hawaii hurricane landfall since Iniki (1992), and quotes Maui County Mayor Bissen on 'storm fatigue.' Attributes the fatality to a car crash per the governor and adds AccuWeather rainfall figures. Most explanatory/backgrounder-style entry.

primary_source_alignment: No primary sources were located for this story. The NHC advisory (issued 11 p.m. local Saturday) is quoted secondhand by NPR, CNN and Newsweek but the underlying document was not provided in the dossier, so direct alignment cannot be verified.

The recurring 'life-threatening flooding and mudslides' quote is attributed to the NHC advisory by NPR, CNN and Newsweek in near-identical wording, suggesting all three drew from the same NHC text rather than independent sourcing.
missing_context: No primary source (NHC advisory text, Hawaiian Electric restoration statement, or the governor's federal emergency request) was included in the dossier, so all official figures are secondhand.
The single Lala fatality is attributed to two different causes (flood per Hawaii Public Radio in NPR; car crash per Gov. Green in Newsweek); no outlet reconciles the discrepancy.

Power-outage figures vary widely and measure different things (peak outages vs. still-without-power), but no outlet clarifies whether the higher numbers are cumulative peaks and the lower is the current residual.
No outlet provides the total dollar cost of Lala damage beyond Newsweek's vague 'millions of dollars.'
The status of the federal emergency declaration Gov. Green requested (NPR) is not followed up on by any outlet.

Newsweek attributes 2026's unusual storm activity to 'an extended El Niño' with warmer waters; no other outlet corroborates this climate framing, and it is presented without cited scientific sourcing.
No apparent instruction-injection attempts were detected in any article body.
brief.suggested_post_type_reason: Four outlets (plus a captions-only AP wire) report the same event with materially different emphases — CNN on climate mechanics, NPR on local impact and politics, Al Jazeera on storm metrics, Newsweek on seasonal/El Niño context — and they diverge on concrete figures like fatality cause, outage counts and wind speeds. That combination of shared core plus divergent framing and unreconciled numbers is a coverage-comparison story, not a straight REPORT.
